rollups.text: Jamie’s multivariable-calculus study, 2024-01-10–2024-02-21: On January 10, Jamie was learning partial derivatives and gradients, aiming for at least 90% on the final; Jamie reported quiz progress from 60% to 78% after three hours of study and homework progress from 65% to 82% over two weeks. By January 24, Jamie had studied directional derivatives and gradient/Hessian optimization, understood the gradient-dot-unit-vector interpretation, reported an 85% quiz score after five hours of study, and improved directional-derivative speed from 20 to 12, then 10 minutes per problem. On February 7, Jamie was studying triple integrals, coordinate transformations, and Jacobians; reported 88% on a quiz about triple integrals and coordinate transformations, and later said triple-integral accuracy was above 90% while time had fallen to 22 minutes per problem. On February 21, Jamie was practicing Jacobians and change of variables, reporting a reduction in Jacobian calculation mistakes from 15% to 5% over two weeks and increased confidence after completing multiple problems.

Jamie’s Jacobian and change-of-variables study, 2024-02-07–2024-02-21: On February 7, Jamie studied Jacobians for triple integrals, spherical and cylindrical coordinates, and volume scaling, including the sphere and unit-cube examples. On February 21, Jamie worked through two-dimensional transformations, polar-coordinate area elements, local area scaling, inverse-function implications, and singular Jacobians; Jamie reported completing five Jacobian problems and feeling confident, later completing seven Jacobian/change-of-variables problems with six correct, and reducing calculation mistakes from 15% to 5% over two weeks.

Jamie’s optimization and Hessian study, 2024-01-24–2024-02-07: On January 24, Jamie moved from gradients and directional derivatives to finding critical points and classifying them with Hessians, using examples including f(x,y)=x²+y²−4x−6y+13 and x²−y². Jamie reported completing seven optimization problems, six correctly, averaging 15 minutes per problem, and asked why critical points need not be minima. On February 7, Jamie revisited the second-derivative test and correctly identified (2,3) as a minimum for the shifted quadratic.

Jamie’s stated learning preferences and study choices: prefers visual, step-by-step explanations for partial derivatives and gradients (2024-01-10); prefers concrete examples before abstract theorems (2024-01-24); requested geometric visualizations for gradient-vector and optimization questions (2024-01-24); requested geometric visualizations for triple integrals and coordinate transformations (2024-02-07); prefers seeing 3D shapes alongside integral calculations (2024-02-07); prefers concrete coordinate transformations before abstract Jacobian theory (2024-02-21); requested graphical illustrations for Jacobian matrices and coordinate transformations (2024-02-21). Jamie decided to use graphing software to visualize level curves and gradient vectors (2024-01-10).

Recurring multivariable-calculus topics Jamie studied: partial derivatives and limit definitions (2024-01-10); gradients, steepest ascent, level curves, and directional derivatives (2024-01-10–2024-02-07); mixed partial derivatives and Clairaut’s theorem (2024-01-10–2024-01-24); critical points, Hessians, and optimization (2024-01-24–2024-02-07); triple integrals and volume (2024-02-07–2024-02-21); coordinate transformations and Jacobian determinants (2024-02-07–2024-02-21); polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates (2024-02-07–2024-02-21).

Reported calculus progress scores and accuracy: Jamie said quiz performance rose from 60% to 78% after three hours of study (2024-01-10); partial-derivative homework rose from 65% to 82% over two weeks (2024-01-10); Jamie scored 85% on a gradient-vectors and directional-derivatives quiz after five hours of study (2024-01-24); scored 88% on a triple-integrals and coordinate-transformations quiz (2024-02-07); reported triple-integral accuracy above 90% (2024-02-07); and reported Jacobian calculation mistakes falling from 15% to 5% over two weeks (2024-02-21).

Reported problem-solving speed improved across topics: Jamie’s directional-derivative time fell from 20 minutes to 12 minutes per problem (2024-01-24), and Jamie later reported an average of 10 minutes per problem while maintaining accuracy (2024-01-24). For triple integrals, Jamie reported an average of 30 minutes per problem (2024-02-07), later 22 minutes while maintaining accuracy above 90% (2024-02-07). For Jacobian and change-of-variables problems, Jamie reported averaging 22 minutes across seven problems (2024-02-21).

Jamie reported completing repeated practice sets: six partial-derivative problems with five correct in 90 minutes (2024-01-10); seven optimization problems with six correct and a 15-minute average (2024-01-24); four triple-integral problems with a 90% average (2024-02-07); six triple-integral problems with five correct and a 30-minute average (2024-02-07); five Jacobian problems with confidence (2024-02-21); and seven Jacobian/change-of-variables problems, with six correct (2024-02-21).

Jamie’s Jacobian and change-of-variables study progressed from triple-integral transformations and visualizing 3D regions on 2024-02-21 to polar-coordinate Jacobians, local area scaling, and vector-field applications on 2024-03-06 (14 days later), then to Jacobians in Green’s theorem on 2024-03-20 (14 days later), and finally to a triple-integral transformation x=uv, y=uw, z=vw on 2024-04-17 (28 days later). Jamie repeatedly sought step-by-step calculations and geometric explanations; the April 17 worked example used incorrect preimage bounds, so its reported value should not be treated as valid.

rollups.text: Jamie’s vector-calculus study developed from learning divergence, curl, and vector fields on 2024-03-06 to applying them to Green’s theorem, circulation, flux, and physical interpretations on 2024-03-20 (14 days later). Topics included source/sink behavior, local rotation, conservative fields, fluid flow, electromagnetism, and visualization. Jamie repeatedly requested concrete, physical explanations and checked calculations, including the zero curl of (yz,xz,xy) and the nonzero curl of (-y,x).
rollups.topic: vector calculus: divergence, curl, and applications

rollups.text: Jamie’s Green’s theorem work began with an intuitive partition-and-cancellation explanation on 2024-03-06, followed by worked line-integral and region examples on 2024-03-20 (14 days later). Jamie practiced identifying P and Q, computing scalar curl, choosing a region and coordinates, and handling orientation, ellipses, polygons, irregular curves, and open or non-simple paths. By 2024-03-20 Jamie reported improved quiz performance but continued to seek help setting up integrals and visualizing regions.

Jamie studied Lagrange multipliers on 2024-04-03, working repeatedly on minimizing x²+y²+z² subject to x+y+z=1 and asking about geometry, classification, and the meaning of λ. Jamie then explored multiple and nonlinear constraints, the sphere-constrained objective xyz, and applications to hypothetical psychological or clinical models. On 2024-04-17 (14 days after the April 3 study), Jamie revisited λ, Hessian verification, faster problem-solving, and critical points of xyz on the unit sphere. Several assistant solutions for xyz omitted axis critical points; the correct full critical-point set has six axis points and eight points with coordinates ±1/√3.

Jamie repeatedly requested visual, step-by-step explanations that combine algebra with geometric or physical interpretations: 3D-shape visualization for integrals and Jacobians (2024-02-21); vector-field visualization, concrete examples, and physical applications (2024-03-06); visualizing Green’s theorem regions, curves, and orientation (2024-03-20); and geometric explanations of constrained optimization (2024-04-03). Jamie mentioned MATLAB, Mathematica, and GeoGebra for visualizing multivariable calculus (2024-02-21); MATLAB, Mathematica, GeoGebra 3D, and Plotly for vector fields (2024-03-06); Python with NumPy and Matplotlib for plotting (2024-03-06); Desmos or GeoGebra for Green’s theorem regions (2024-03-20); and Python plotting code for constrained optimization (2024-04-03). These were preferences and tools discussed, not evidence that Jamie installed or used them.

Jamie’s recurring applied interests included fluid flow and airflow (2024-03-06 and 2024-03-20), electromagnetism and laboratory field examples (2024-03-06 and 2024-03-20), and clinical ventilation or hospital-room CFD (2024-03-06). Jamie asked about OpenFOAM and ParaView setup and visualization on 2024-03-06, and later requested a hospital-room ventilation simulation in ANSYS Fluent. These were interests and requests; the records do not confirm that Jamie completed a simulation or installed the software.

Jamie reported vector-field practice on 2024-03-06: 6 problems at 88% with 18 minutes per problem; later 8 problems, 7 correct, at 20 minutes per problem; and 10 problems at 15 minutes per problem. Jamie also reported reducing curl/divergence calculation errors from 20% to 7% over the preceding three weeks. The records show increasing reported practice volume and faster average times, but do not establish that every metric came from the same problem set.

rollups.text: Jamie reported Lagrange-multiplier practice on 2024-04-03 as 5 problems averaging 90%, later also reporting five problems at 90% and 30 minutes per problem; Jamie said three practice sessions raised a quiz score from 75% to 88%. On 2024-04-17 Jamie again reported five constrained-optimization problems at 90% and 30 minutes per problem, and separately reported completing 8 constrained-optimization problems with an average time of 28 minutes per problem. These are separate reports, not necessarily cumulative totals.

Jamie’s multivariable-calculus study progressed from Jacobians and change of variables on 2024-04-17 to broader review of gradients, directional derivatives, integrals, Green’s theorem, Hessians, and constrained optimization on 2024-05-15. Jamie repeatedly sought stepwise algebra supported by geometric intuition, visualizations, and applied examples, and requested that comprehensive explanations integrate multiple concepts. By 2024-05-15 Jamie reported a 96% final practice-test score and asked how to prepare for comprehensive problems despite limited prior review of the full range of topics. Elapsed time: 28 days.

Jamie’s Jacobian/change-of-variables learning thread began with triple-integral volume scaling and transformed limits on 2024-04-17, including the maps x=u²−v², y=2uv, z=w or z=uw, and x=uv, y=uw, z=vw. Jamie continued asking about validity, injectivity, transformed regions, spherical coordinates, area and volume scaling, and applications to MRI registration through 2024-05-15. Jamie requested stepwise calculations and geometric visualizations and reported triple-integral problem time improving to 30 minutes on 2024-04-17. Elapsed time: 28 days.

Jamie’s constrained-optimization study included Lagrange multipliers, gradient geometry, Hessian classification, multiple constraints, inequality/KKT conditions, and multiplier sensitivity. On 2024-04-17 Jamie reported improving Lagrange-system setup errors from 20% to 7% over two weeks and asked about the meaning of λ. On 2024-05-01 Jamie was still finding multiple constraints and sensitivity difficult; on 2024-05-15 Jamie continued reviewing the method alongside gradients and directional derivatives. Elapsed time: 28 days.

Reported constrained-optimization practice and assessment milestones: 2024-04-17, five Lagrange practice problems averaging 90%; 2024-04-17, six Lagrange problems with five correct, averaging 32 minutes each; 2024-04-17, score rose from 75% to 88% after three practice sessions; 2024-05-01, five constrained-optimization problems averaging 91% and 35 minutes each; 2024-05-01, seven problems with six correct, averaging 40 minutes each; 2024-05-01, score rose from 80% to 92% after four practice sessions; 2024-05-01, nine constrained-optimization problems averaging 35 minutes each; 2024-05-15, ten mixed-topic problems with nine correct; 2024-05-15, reported 93% on a final practice test; 2024-05-15, later reported 96% after additional review sessions.

Jamie reported several distinct practice totals for constrained optimization: five problems on 2024-04-17; six on 2024-04-17; five on 2024-05-01; seven on 2024-05-01; nine on 2024-05-01; and ten mixed-topic problems on 2024-05-15. These are separate session reports, not a deduplicated cumulative total.

Reported average time per problem changed across sessions: triple-integral change-of-variables problems took about 35 minutes on 2024-04-17, improving to 30 minutes by 2024-04-17; constrained-optimization practice was reported at 32 minutes per problem on 2024-04-17, 40 minutes on 2024-05-01, and about 35 minutes on 2024-05-01 and 2024-05-15. The reports refer to different problem sets and should not be read as one uniform trend.

Recurring learning preferences Jamie expressed: stepwise calculations; visual and geometric explanations; concrete worked examples; graphing/visualization tools; physical or applied interpretations; and algebra paired with geometric intuition for complex constrained-optimization problems. Jamie also requested that comprehensive explanations integrate multiple concepts and that Jacobian triple-integral answers include stepwise calculations and geometric visualizations.

Recurring applications Jamie explored or asked about included clinical psychology data fitting, psychological-model parameter fitting, clinical treatment parameters, and resource allocation. These were discussed as prospective applications or hypothetical examples; no specific real clinical model or dataset was supplied.
